system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 13 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-10-26 17:52:00 to 2177-11-08 13:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with morbid obesity, steroid-dependent psoriatic arthritis, insulin-dependent diabetes, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted from a rehabilitation facility due to recurrent episodes of hypoxemia, palpitations, and concern for pulmonary embolism. Initial evaluation ruled out new clots, but the patient had a subtherapeutic INR and a history of warfarin resistance. He was treated with heparin and carefully transitioned back to warfarin, with hematology input. Hypoxemia episodes were attributed to fluid overload and sleep apnea; he was diuresed from 386 to 366 lbs with improvement. A positive blood culture was deemed contaminated, and antibiotics were discontinued. His left leg wound showed signs of healing without active infection. A brief unresponsive episode prompted ICU evaluation and psychiatry consultation, resulting in a diagnosis of adjustment disorder with anxious features. The PICC line was removed due to safety concerns. Pain management was optimized with OxyContin and azathioprine restart. He was discharged home with services, on therapeutic anticoagulation, with follow-up arranged across multiple specialties.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Secondary diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, not stated as uncontrolled, or unspecified
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ was admitted to ___ on ___ for recurrent LLE 
cellulitis. He had originally presented in ___ 
with LLE cellulitis without known source. His initial 
presentation was concerning for necrotizing fasciitis and 
required debridement (which did not identify fasciitis). He 
later developed a PE during his rehabiliation process, and has 
been repeatedly admitted for wound and cellulitic complications. 
His hospital course for this admission is summarized as follows:

1) Cellulitis - Exam on admission demonstrating cellulitis at 
proximal margin of LLE ulcer. Patient had leukocytosis but no 
other components of SIRS criteria on admission. Of note, his 
leukocytosis was likely not secondary to chronic corticosteroid 
use, as review of past records demonstrated persistently normal 
WBC depsite 4.5mg dexamethasone daily. He was started on broad 
empiric coverage with vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, 
giving his recurrent admissions and diabetes. His azathioprine 
was discontinued, as his surgical wound was still failing to 
heal at a normal rate, and the wound was the most likely source 
of cellulitis. ID was consulted, and recommended transitioning 
to ceftriaxone given the Streptococcal appearance of the rash 
(rather than Staphylococcal). Mr. ___ began to improve with 
this regimen, though day to day physical exam findings 
fluctuated. He underwent a CT scan on ___ demonstrating 
multiple new fluid/air-containing collections in the 
anteromedial and medial aspect of the upper left calf, the 
largest of which measured up to 4.5 x 1.8 cm. The acute care 
surgical service was consulted. At that time no intervention was 
performed, due to patient's previous poor wound healing 
following surgical intervention; conservative management was 
indicated pending worsening or clinical deterioration. The 
patient then developed worsening pain and swelling over the next 
few days. A LLE ultrasound on ___ demonstrated large 
subcutaneous fluid collections in the cellulitic area; ACS then 
performed an I+D on the same day with significant return of 
pus-like discharge. The patient then improved significantly over 
the next several days. His pain medication requirement 
diminished as he improved. A PICC line was placed, and he was 
eventually discharged with home OPAT to continue ceftriaxone 2g 
IV daily and follow-up in ID clinc with Dr. ___ on 
___.

recovery from LLE debridement. Goal INR ___, taking 10mg and

warfarin per day throughout his stay. Warfarin dose on discharge 
= 10mg per day.

home. Stopped azathioprine after discussion with outpatient 
rheumatologist. Undoubtedly contributing to poor healing of his 
ulcer. Will need follow-up with rheumatology as outpatient prior

at home. Received 16u qam, 33u qpm glargine with self-correction 
using sliding scale and carbohydrate counting. Patient very 
adept at this method of glucose control at blood sugars well 
controlled during his stay.

5) OSA - continued CPAP. Patient has frequent ventricular ectopy 
as noticed on nightly telemetry, but was cardiovascularly stable 
throughout admission.

6) HLD - Continued atorvastatin.

7) HTN - continued lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’ve been admitted for worsening redness and swelling near your left leg wound. Can you tell me when it started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it started a couple evenings ago—redness creeping up from the wound, more pain, especially when I move my leg. It’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned increased tingling too, despite your usual neuropathy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, more than usual. Not numb—actually more sensitive. I’m worried it’s infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. Your exam shows redness and warmth around the ulcer, and your white blood cell count is elevated. We’ll start antibiotics right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be IV? My last infection needed a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start IV vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam for broad coverage. We’ll reassess in a few days. Also, your INR is high—4.5—so we’re holding warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had trouble with warfarin before—doses all over the place. Should I be worried about clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. No signs of bleeding. Once your INR comes down, we’ll restart warfarin at a stable dose—likely 10 mg daily based on past records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my psoriatic arthritis meds—should I keep taking azathioprine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped azathioprine for now. It may be slowing wound healing, and with active infection, we want to reduce immunosuppression. Your rheumatologist agrees.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been on so many of those drugs—nothing works long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll follow up with rheumatology after you’ve healed. For now, focus on treating this infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat ultrasound didn’t show a drainable collection yesterday, but we’re still concerned. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Worse, actually. More swelling, and it’s hotter to the touch. I’m really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ordering a CT scan today to get a better look. If there’s an abscess, we may need to drain it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows new fluid and air pockets in your calf—some up to 4.5 cm. It’s concerning for abscess formation. We’ve consulted surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s worse? Do they want to operate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not major surgery. They recommend incision and drainage if things worsen. For now, we’re continuing antibiotics and watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your infection isn’t improving. Pain and swelling are increasing. Surgery will drain the fluid tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous? I’ve had trouble healing before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s necessary. Leaving it could lead to worse infection. They’ll make small incisions, drain the pus, and pack it lightly. Healing should follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’ll stay on antibiotics after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Infectious disease reviewed your case. We’re switching from vancomycin to IV ceftriaxone—better for the type of infection you likely have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it staph again? The culture last time said MSSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, MSSA—methicillin-sensitive staph. Ceftriaxone covers that well. You’ll get it through a PICC line after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the PICC line safety talk last time. I’ll be careful. My wife will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll have a nurse go over care again before discharge. No adjusting it yourself—only trained staff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. They drained pus from two areas. You should start feeling better in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It already feels less tight. How long until the antibiotics are done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with 14 days of IV ceftriaxone. A nurse will come daily. Follow-up with infectious disease in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I’ve been managing it myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sugars have been well-controlled on your usual glargine dose with sliding scale. Keep doing what you’re doing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your white count is coming down. From 12.9 to 9.4. Infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. And the warfarin? My INR was 2.1 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back in range. We’ve kept you on 10 mg daily. That’s what’s working. We’ll send you home on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Staying on warfarin is key. We’ll monitor INR regularly as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving. You’re using less morphine. We’ll switch you to your baseline dose soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on extra MS Contin since the drainage. How long should I stay on it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper it as your pain decreases. You’re discharged with a 3-week supply. After that, go back to your usual dose unless pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And hydromorphone for breakthrough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 60 pills for breakthrough. Use sparingly. We want to avoid long-term opioid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge in two days. You’re afebrile, wound is draining less, and labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infectious disease in two weeks, rheumatology soon after, and plastic surgery for the chronic ulcer. We’ll send referrals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have that rash on my right arm. Is it fungal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re adding miconazole cream twice daily. If it doesn't improve, see your dermatologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: Discharge tomorrow morning. PICC nurse will train you and your wife on care. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—what signs should make me call the doctor or go back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, increased redness or pain, more drainage, shortness of breath, chest pain, or if you feel generally worse. Call ID or come to ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the PICC line leaks or gets dislodged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cover it with a clean dressing and call the home health nurse immediately. Don’t touch it yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR is 2.3—perfect. All labs are stable. You’re cleared for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your meds, wound care, and PICC instructions one more time. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, before I leave—can I restart azathioprine after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Wait until you see rheumatology. We need to make sure the infection is fully gone and the wound is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in before discharge. You look well—alert, walking independently, wound looks much improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better than I have in weeks. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: antibiotics for 14 days, keep all follow-ups, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve got my list and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re discharged home with services. Take care, Mr. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, diabetes, morbid obesity, and a chronic left leg ulcer was admitted for recurrent cellulitis with worsening erythema, pain, and swelling near the wound site. He was started on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics due to leukocytosis and concern for deep infection. Imaging revealed new fluid and air collections in the left calf, prompting surgical consultation. After clinical deterioration, he underwent incision and drainage of a subcutaneous abscess. Antibiotics were narrowed to IV ceftriaxone based on infectious disease recommendation, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient therapy. His warfarin was held initially due to an elevated INR of 4.5 but was restarted at 10 mg daily, achieving therapeutic anticoagulation. Azathioprine was discontinued to support wound healing. The patient improved clinically, with resolving infection, stable diabetes control, and reduced pain. He was discharged home with a 14-day course of IV antibiotics, follow-up arranged in infectious disease, rheumatology, and plastic surgery, and detailed instructions on PICC line safety and warning signs.
